HEADLINE: Uranus bodes ill for Tony Abbott
INTRO: Ides or no ides, March promises to be interesting.
TEXT:
Ides or no ides, March promises to be interesting.

It's only been two weeks since Prime Minister Tony Abbott saw off a bruising attempt to remove him and already the crystal-ball gazing has begun to pick the timing of the next attempt on his leadership.

But not everybody thinks Abbott's prime ministership is terminal.

Milton Black, a well-known astrologer who says many politicians and economists seek his predictions, says Abbott will lead the Coalition to the 2016 election and win with a reduced majority. Malcolm Turnbull and Julie Bishop will not be contenders for the leadership and Joe Hockey will remain Treasurer.

The problem, as always, is Uranus. Mr Abbott, a Scorpio, can expect the hardest 2½ years of stress and difficulty in his destiny because Saturn is returning to the same position at the time of his birth, while Uranus is moving to an "opposition" position that will test his leadership abilities.

It's all bad news for Labor leader Bill Shorten, a Taurus, while Pluto (destruction) clashes with Mars (attitude), according to his astrological chart.

"He will lose public support by the 2016 election for not giving the electorate any assurance of how he will handle the present and ongoing deficit, without squeezing the taxpayer," Black says.

Superstitious types will be wary of March 15, the "Ides of March" when Brutus dispatched Julius Caesar, but modern day oracles such as conservative News Corp columist Andrew Bolt have picked March 3 as the day of destiny.

Next Tuesday is the the next Liberal Party meeting in Canberra when dissaffected MPs could push for Abbott to either step down or face a challenge for his job.

Abbott supporters say it is Turnbull's last chance to push to be prime minister because Abbott has had a small bounce in the opinion polls following his national security address last Monday, and there are only three more parliamentary weeks left until the NSW state election on March 28.

NSW Liberals want the uncertainty cleared up one way or another within the next two weeks to give Liberal Premier Mike Baird a chance to sell his brand of conservative politics without the distraction of federal leadership squabbles.

On the other side of politics, Labor insiders think a spill is still weeks away and they are rooting for Abbott to prevail over Turnbull.

"The Liberals don't have the testicles for it unlike Labor which doesn't mind the sight of blood," according to one gleeful Labor strategist.

The tension is causing headaches for all concerned. Social Services Minister and potential leadership rival Scott "Sco Mo" Morrison described the ructions as "a bit of political bed-wetting" and he wasn't anticipating a sinister "visit in the night".

Assistant Treasurer Josh Frydenberg accidentally said Turnbull had been a "good PM", and Joe Hockey had to keep smiling at an Australian Jewish News function in Sydney on Thursday where local member Malcolm Turnbull was described as "Australia's next prime minister".

Thankfully some stability still exists. Nationals leader Warren Truss said the Nationals had an agreement with Abbott to form a Coalition government and "if there were to be some change, well then that agreement would obviously have to be renewed".

HEADLINE: Liberal sniping spooks donors
INTRO: Businessman Richard Smith has suspended donations to the Liberal Party, while Queensland resources entrepreneur Peter Bond wants Treasurer Joe Hockey replaced in a cabinet shake-up.
TEXT:
Businessman Richard Smith has suspended donations to the Liberal Party, while Queensland resources entrepreneur Peter Bond wants Treasurer Joe Hockey replaced in a cabinet shake-up.

Mr Smith, who is worth $830 million and built his fortune from PFD Food Services, said the Coalition had made "an absolute balls of it" and he was "fed up with giving them money".

"It annoys you that they sort of get side-tracked from running the country by who is going to lead the party," he said. "It's all about them and not what's best for the country."

Leaked emails this week exposed the anger of long-time fundraiser Philip Higginson about the way the party was being run. The tensions look likely to turn off many donors.

Bond, the founder of Linc Energy and whose wealth is estimated at $280 million, donated $100,000 to the Liberal Party last year. He wants Mr Abbott to lift his performance and is calling for a cabinet shake-up.

"Personally, I am a supporter of Tony Abbott and I think he's a good man, but it comes down to performance and I think he really needs to perform.

"I would have preferred to see an Abbott-Turnbull combination. Hockey is a good guy but I think Turnbull would be better as Treasurer."

"Politicians are paid to do deals and get a budget through. They need to start doing this. I think Abbott probably needs to shake up the whole cabinet."

Mr Abbott's leadership woes have been compounded by the leaking of damaging emails about the interplay between the political and organisational wings of the Liberal Party.

The party's honorary federal treasurer Phil Higginson sent an explosive email to members of his federal executive in which he said the fact Mr Abbott's chief of staff, Peta Credlin, was married to Liberal Party federal director Brian Loughnane created an untenable conflict.

"Conflicts of interests only have to be perceived to be frowned upon and to be highly damaging," he wrote. "They don't actually have to occur."

Mr Higginson refused to sign off on the latest accounts for four months as he fought with Mr Loughnane for access. Mr Abbott called the leak a "storm in a teacup".

One Liberal Party stalwart who asked not to be named said the leaks would harm fundraising."This is hugely destructive because it gives people excuses and people don't need much of an excuse not to donate to a political party. It has really damaged the fundraising effort. It also raises issues - well, how are you spending my money and what are you up to? The Labor Party probably can't believe their luck that all of this is happening on the Liberal side."

Some Liberal members expressed misgivings about Mr Turnbull, the frontrunner to replace Mr Abbott.

"People used to say if you like Kevin Rudd, don't meet him," one senior Liberal Party member said. "The same applies to Malcolm Turnbull. If you like him, don't meet him."

Mr Smith is a long-time donor to the Liberal Party, believing the party is best placed to run the economy and country. He gave $15,000 last year.

Despite his frustration with the government's performance at present, he supports Mr Abbott over Mr Turnbull and would never back Bill Shorten.

"I was fed up giving them money. When you give money to charity you like to think they're going to do something with it. You give money to the Liberal Party and they're making a mess of it, an absolute balls of it."

Business SA chief executive Nigel McBride said the state's business community wanted an end to instability.

"My members are clearly concerned about the instability in the federal government because ultimately that instability undermines the government's reform agenda," he said.

"The vast majority . . . feel we need strong economic reform and bold leadership at a federal level. Obviously any leadership instability undermines that. There's a concern that the federal government will become somewhat more timid than they've been and that's not good for the business community," Mr McBride said.

HEADLINE: Cabinet resists second spill
INTRO: Malcolm Turnbull would stand should the Liberal Party leadership be declared vacant, but he has no intention of forcing the issue by either challenging or resigning from the frontbench, his supporters have been told.
TEXT:
Malcolm Turnbull would stand should the Liberal Party leadership be declared vacant, but he has no intention of forcing the issue by either challenging or resigning from the frontbench, his supporters have been told.

Coalition backbenchers agitating for a leadership change believe the cabinet must precipitate the next move against Tony Abbott by resigning from the frontbench if necessary.

"It has to come from the frontbench this time. The lobbying must be done by the principals," said one Liberal clsoe to the backbench-driven push to oust Mr Abbott three weeks ago.

Resignations by key frontbenchers, including by Mr Abbott, were used to tear down Mr Turnbull's leadership in 2009 and a repeat of the tactic has been put to both Mr Turnbull and Julie Bishop as an option to force Mr Abbott to go. Neither has any intention of doing so, but both are now expected to run for the leadership should a new spill motion be carried and the leadership be declared vacant.

Cabinet ministers played down the significance of a renewed push on Friday and said there was little likelihood of a spill happening next week. But there was an obvious split at the highest levels over who had the right to dump a prime minister - his colleagues or the voters.

Social Services Minister Scott Morrison, who stands to become either treasurer or deputy leader should there be a leadership coup, disputed Mr Abbott's earlier assertions that only the voters had the right to remove an elected prime minister.

"These things are the gift of the party room and, remember, our party room is made up of people who are elected by their constituents, so that's how the system works and I think anyone who pretends differently is kidding themselves," Mr Morrison said.

Ms Bishop concurred: "It is self-evident that the individual members of the party room are able to elect the leader and the deputy leader of the Liberal Party. That has always been the case and I imagine it will continue to be the case," she said.

Late on Friday in New Zealand, Mr Abbott softened his line, saying his job was "the subject of the party room and the subject of the electorate.

"I am looking forward to having the confidence of both," he said.

Treasurer Joe Hockey, who will be swept aside in the event of a coup, disagreed with Mr Morrison and Ms Bishop.

"It's the Australian people that have the right to remove a prime minister, not anyone else," Mr Hockey said.

He slammed those in his own ranks and in the media who were fomenting the unrest, saying they were motivated by self-interest.

"It's about the self-interest of some, whether they're reporting the news or whether they're actually in the party and thinking that somehow they'll advance if there's change," he said.

Supporters of Mr Abbott claim that if another spill was instigated, the numbers from three weeks ago, in which Mr Abbott held on by 61 votes to 39, would be about the same.

But this was hotly contested by the agents for change, who claimed Mr Turnbull was already sitting on about 60 of the 102 total votes.

Everyone agreed that there was no method or co-ordination behind the latest apparent push. "It's in complete disarray," one minister said. "It's a clusterf***," said another.

Despite the obvious divisions in cabinet, there was next to no support among ministers on Friday to precipitate a move next week or soon after that. Ministers believed it would be a premature and unedifying move so soon after the last spill, when it was agreed Mr Abbott should be given time.

"I think what we might be seeing here is a bit of political bed-wetting by some, and frankly we've got to get past that," Mr Morrison said.

"What you're seeing here is a bit of low-level rumbling and trying to talk itself up."

Another minister, who supports a leadership change but asked not to be named, said with regard to the cabinet initiating something next week: "We're seriously not interested.

"It's got to be fair, it's got to look like we gave him a go."

Others posited that the latest push was driven by a touch of panic among the dissidents after the Newspoll published this week showed a slight improvement for the Coalition.

The preferred course of action is for Mr Abbott to come to the realisation some time after the May budget that he cannot win the election, and resign. This is most unlikely.

Another factor mitigating against a rush to revisit the leadership is a fear of a backlash from the electorate, which is hostile to the concept of a sitting prime minister being dumped. MPs report that there is a dislike of Mr Abbott among voters but also disillusionment about the Coalition going down the same path as Labor. The scenario of changing leaders has been further complicated by a widespread acceptance that Ms Bishop would run for the top job herself, leaving it unclear as to the structure of the new team. The most likely scenario would be Mr Turnbull as leader, Ms Bishop as deputy and Mr Morrison as treasurer.

Mr Morrison, who was talking to Fairfax Radio, was candid when asked about his longer-term leadership ambitions and his bona fides.

"Anyone who goes into Parliament who says that they don't aspire to do as much as they can in politics is lying to you," he said.

"I'm a fixer, I get things done and that's what I look to do in this portfolio and in welfare."

HEADLINE: Blackmores considers cannabis
INTRO: Alternative medicine firm Blackmores wants to supply cannabis to the NSW government.
TEXT:
Alternative medicine firm Blackmores wants to supply cannabis to the NSW government.

BioCeuticals, part of Blackmores group, has told The Children's Hospital at Westmead it wants to supply drugs for a NSW government-sponsored clinical trial of cannabis in paediatric epilepsy. BioCeuticals managing director Nathan Cheong said there was "a groundswell of anecdotal benefits" for treatment of drug-resistant epilepsy in children using "cannabidiol-enriched cannabis" and rigorous testing was needed before it could be sold to the public. "The investigation is at a very early stage and would strictly require professional dispensing within a hospital setting. We believe it is important to assess the safety and efficacy of this ingredient," he said.

Dan Haslam, the Tamworth-man whose public use of cannabis to treat his pain played a crucial role in shifting opinion in NSW died at 25 from bowel cancer this week.

NSW has as an interim measure created a register of terminally ill cannabis users who will be protected from prosecution.

In the past month 25 terminally ill cannabis users and 57 carers have applied to be placed on the list. Drug-resistant epilepsy can significantly disrupt the lives of affected children.

GEOFF WINESTOCK

HEADLINE: Tax officials like 'benevolent dictators'
INTRO: Senior tax officials, who can use discretion to resolve taxpayers' disputes, have been described as a "benevolent dictatorship" which should be replaced by a more transparent and independent arbiter of disputes between the Australian Taxation Office and small businesses and individual taxpayers.
TEXT:
Senior tax officials, who can use discretion to resolve taxpayers' disputes, have been described as a "benevolent dictatorship" which should be replaced by a more transparent and independent arbiter of disputes between the Australian Taxation Office and small businesses and individual taxpayers.

The Abbott government is considering a recommendation by the Inspector-General of Taxation to introduce a separate and independent appeals group headed a second commissioner appointed by the government, rather than the tax commissioner, to hear the complaints before they reach the courts.

It comes after Inspector-General Ali Noroozi found many taxpayers felt their complaints were not considered objectively by the ATO.

Mr Noroozi said the view was supported by the ATO's own statistics which found 85 per cent of taxpayer disputes were resolved without a court hearing once they reached the Administrative Appeals Tribunal.

He said the ATO had arguably the least separation between its original decision makers - who assess the initial tax bill - and the officers who review the decisions at the taxpayer's request, compared to other countries with similar tax authorities.

"It is therefore not surprising that many taxpayers felt that their cases were not being independently reviewed and that the system was not treating them fairly and equitably."

The idea of splitting the tax office's revenue-collecting activities from its appeals function was first raised by Mr Noroozi in 2011 and by Treasurer Joe Hockey before the 2013 federal election.

There have been suggestions a separate administration should be created to represent the highest levels of independence but Mr Noroozi said there were difficulties associated with this option including increased costs and overlaps with existing bodies such as the AAT.

HEADLINE: Voting with their feet: why the sporty set is ditching the gym
INTRO: The industry is itself struggling to get into shape post-GFC.
TEXT:
The industry is itself struggling to get into shape post-GFC.

Hot yoga studio owner Shannon Barry's biggest challenge has been his success. More students mean growth, and finding studio space around pricey inner suburbs, as well as more teachers, is not easy.

Nevertheless, his Sohis Grass Roots Yoga business, which opened in Melbourne's St Kilda three years ago, has established another branch.

Barry now trains teachers, running a "mindful yoga" teaching academy to ensure there's enough supply of instructors to meet demand.

More than 30 years since Hollywood actress and fitness pioneer Jane Fonda sold 17 million videos cheering on baby-boomers to star-jump and high-kick their way to health, the fitness industry is facing its biggest challenge.

Industry revenue across Australia, at $1.3 billion, is up on the previous year, but a fraction of what it was at the high point of almost $10 billon in 2008, reports Ibis World Australia.

As the GFC hit, people trimmed their spending and ended their gym contracts as soon as they could.

Dominant player Fitness First has endured a $910 million restructure and four years of declining revenue growth, while low-cost upstarts Anytime Australia and Jetts Fitness have racked up an impressive market share running on wafer-thin margins. Anytime is now Australia's biggest fitness player.

But it's not just low-cost operators causing the major gym chains to break into a sweat. An even bigger threat lurks in the likes of personal trainers such as Mark Antony. Antony says he could work out of a gym but renting his small studio space is more cost-effective. And clients are over gyms.

"It's good for people who don't want to work out in front of others in a big gym - it's just me and my client," Antony says of his garage-style space, also near fitness-obsessed St Kilda.

Time-poor consumers are looking to multi-task with their fitness regime - burn fat and chew it at the same. "They like being outdoors, but they also like being able to talk to one another," says Sydney-based trainer Rory Boyden.

In his five years of personal training his customers have moved out of mega-gyms, into parks and now into tiny spaces like the boxy room in Edgecliff Road in Sydney's eastern suburbs where he conducts Cross Fit classes. Cross Fit is a souped-up libertarian take on aerobics involving "functional fitness" tasks like dragging truck tyres. It was founded by Greg Glassman, a scholar of economists Milton Friedman and Friedrich Hayek and a self-described "rabid libertarian".

"At Cross Fit you get allocated rest breaks, which means that people get to know each other and get to have a good chat while recovering.

"People have moved away from sitting on a bike and pedalling for an hour or hanging out in a gym by themselves pumping weights, mainly because of boredom, but there's a lack of results too," he says.

Yoga teacher Barry has expanded to three studios and is now hunting for a fourth space in the coveted South Melbourne area.

He attributes the success of his business to a community-focused philosophy, which he says taps into people's desire for a sense of coming together - something young professionals struggle to find.

The trend to socialising while exercising helps explain the exponential rise of Tough Mudder - a 16-plus obstacle race involving skips of iced water and fields of electrified wire. "It makes people feel really good about themselves afterwards," UK founder Will Dean tells AFR Weekend.

HEADLINE: Labor folds on opposing trawl of metadata
INTRO: Australia's corporate watchdogs will have wide-reaching power to trawl through email, telephone and internet records under a last-minute deal between Labor and the government to enact a controversial data-retention law.
TEXT:
Australia's corporate watchdogs will have wide-reaching power to trawl through email, telephone and internet records under a last-minute deal between Labor and the government to enact a controversial data-retention law.

The deal will outrage civil libertarian groups, and internet service providers say the $400 million plan could lead to higher prices for customers, after Labor backed down from its opposition.

The Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security on Friday recommended additional safeguards be added to the law including oversight by the Commonwealth Ombudsman, a mandatory breach-notification scheme for privacy and data breaches, protections for journalists' sources and a "substantial contribution" by the government to the telecommunications sector to implement the changes.

The government has kept the centrepiece of the law that would force telecommunications providers to store the metadata of all phone and internet users for two years.

"The cost which has been put forward suggests that the regime might vary between roughly $200 million and $400 million to be implemented; the committee has made recommendations to the government of how we should go about trying to work with industry to ensure the government makes a significant contribution to that cost," Liberal committee chair Dan Tehan said.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission and the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission were both originally not going to have access to the powers but under the deal, will join other crime-fighting bodies including the Australian Federal Police as enforcement agencies entitled to access the metadata of all Australians without a warrant, after lobbying by the regulators.

ASIC has been publicly arguing the powers are "absolutely essential" to fight white-collar crime and told a parliamentary committee its existing telecommunications powers were essential in their successful insider trading cases again NAB insider trader, Lukus Kamay and Hanlong Mining executive Bo Shi Zhu, as well as its investigation into the $176 million collapse of Trio Capital.

The ACCC will gain the powers, despite not making a submission to the inquiry. ACCC chairman Rod Sims said the watchdog lobbied behind the scenes to ensure his agency was also included.

"These powers are crucial, particularly for tackling cartels," Mr Sims said. "Most of our cartel cases we have got hold of phone records. So, you need that."

Metadata can include everything from basic phone call statistics to specific information like the location of a smartphone user when they access the internet but the committee's report said the Explanatory Memorandum should spell out it does not capture PINs, passwords, content or web-browser histories. The plan caused headlines after Attorney-General George Brandis badly struggled to explain the proposal live on Sky News last August. As it stands, law-enforcement and intelligence agencies are able to access metadata - who we call and who calls us, as well as internet records - without a warrant. That will continue under the Telecommunications Interception and Access Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014.

Agencies said the new laws were meant to ensure the "status quo" remained but that telecommunications companies continued to store phone and internet records and didn't delete them as some have done when they no longer require them.

The committee has been scrutinising the bill since December, holding public hearings where it heard from civil liberties, privacy, media and lawyer groups that the laws needed to change or be scrapped. Law-enforcement and intelligence agencies also attended, but said they believed the legislation was sound and did not need to be altered.

Key pointsProviders to store users' metadata for two years

ASIC argues scrutiny 'absolutely essential'

HEADLINE: Bond-like stocks: the 'Telstrafication' of the sharemarket
INTRO: As investors turn to equities for a bond-like fix, some stocks have been bid up to excessive levels.
TEXT:
As investors turn to equities for a bond-like fix, some stocks have been bid up to excessive levels.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management's head of Australian equities Dion Hershan is blunt. We are in the midst of a massive distortion of the equity market.

"Valuations for some stocks in the REIT, infrastructure, telco, utilities and healthcare industries at the moment don't make sense and are only justified by spot bond yields"

Hershan, who learnt the investing trade at Columbia University - a temple of value-investing - is one of a number of investors that are growing weary of an excessive reach for yield in the face of historically low bond rates.

Yet as the belief grows that interest rates in Australia will converge with the rest of the world and linger in low rate limbo for years to come, the faith of value investors - who try to spot bargains by buying stocks based on the fundamental worth of the underlying business - is being tested.

This is a new world, where companies are valued not by the worth of their businesses but their ability to spit out cash. No stock exemplifies this more than Telstra, which has traded tick for tick with the long-term bond rate.

The telco now has a dividend yield of about 4.7 per cent, below the 6.5 per cent average since it floated. Against a 2.5 per cent long-term bond rate, the stock might still look cheap, but on more traditional valuation methods such as P/E ratios it now trades at 19 times earnings. But it's not just Telstra - the utilities, property and healthcare - are sectors which have been bid up by investors seeking solace from dwindling cash rates in defensive high-yielding shares.

How did we get to this point? In response to the financial crisis, central banks have cut interest rates to levels few could have imagined. They were supposed to stoke the animal spirits, to compel companies to use cheap financing to invest in plants and employ workers. But it's had the opposite effect. An ever larger pool of savers faced with low rates, have been forced to turned to the sharemarket for income, compelling and rewarding companies that look and act like a dull old bond.

Hershan is underweight "yield" - more specifically utilities, REITS and telecoms - where investors are buying shares for their bond-like qualities. He says the weight of money chasing yields means he might not be proved right in this quarter or the next, but eventually the position will be rewarded. "We don't have a view on when rates will go up and we don't know when we will be vindicated but history tells us this can't go on forever," he says.

Another high-profile investor warning about the distortive forces of the bond market is Magellan's Hamish Douglass, who recently told AFR Weekend the US bond market, which sets the tone for rates around the world, was being mis-read.

With a view towards an eventual rate hike by the US Federal Reserve and a rise in 10-year US bond rates from 2 to about 4.5 per cent, he is taking the view that expensive defensive stocks will eventually lose favour relative to cyclicals. The view among investors concerned about the excesses of yield chasing is that long-term bond rates will eventually rise. This will expose the folly of overpaying for businesses simply based on the generosity of their dividend policy.

"The big driver for Australian stocks in 2014 was what happened in the bond market and most of the move can be explained by the long bond rate moving from 4 per cent to 2.5 per cent," says Hershan. "Investors should be careful not to assume that just because the front end has declined that long term bond rates will stay low."

The old Keynesian adage that the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent can be tweaked for value investors: The yield hunt can persist for longer than they can retain the faith of their investors.

The challenge for investors is that the "lower for longer" interest rate thesis could take hold and ensure that the search for yield swamps good old fundamental valuation in the mind of the market for years to come.

London-based consultant Ian Harnett of Absolute Strategies Research has has pinned the blame on central bank policy for forcing companies to "look and act like bonds". Rather than using low rates to invest in their businesses, yield-starved investors have encouraged management to borrow to buy back stock and return more cash. He's also warning the distortion could persist for a decade or longer in the absence of rising interest rates. With a rate rise in Europe not expected until the end of the decade, yield-rich stocks could remain elevated. The era of the "nifty fifties" lasted right through the 1960s and into the early 70s as investors paid extraordinary multiples for 50 large cap defensive stocks - in the face of low interest rates. That's eerily similar to the forces at play now. The experience of Japan is another historical warning that the war of attrition between value and yield could be a long one.

Gerard Minack of Minack Advisors says the Western world is turning decidedly Japanese. "I watched Japan in the 1990s and the cemetery is full of people who tried to short their bonds," he says. "The last four or five years we've filled the cemetery with people who are trying to be bearish on treasuries and bonds, so rates lower for longer is the take-away."

But Minack warns that the data shows that a point can be reached when falling bond rates no longer support the sharemarket. "There is such a thing as too much of a good thing," he says. "For most of our careers we've associated falling bond yield with higher equity valuations. We went from very high bond yields to lower ones and valuations tend to go up but further declines in bonds won't necessarily help equity valuations."

In Australia, Minack sees the "yield pain trade" that has pushed up telco, utilities and healthcare stocks will continue - as more mums and dads switch from term deposits into bank shares in the face of "crummy" rates.

"Now that's befuddling some people who are looking at these banks which are among the most expensive in the world. I am not saying you should buy banks. My point is that if yields stay low, that process will probably make them into a bigger bubble."

Hershan may be warning of a yield-driven distortion, but he is an owner of the banks which he believes represent value in the traditional sense.

"It would be naïve to believe the banks aren't a beneficiary [of lower yields] but the starting point is that these stocks were cheap by comparison. The banks have growth and dividends whereas other yield-centric sectors probably don't," says Hershan.

While he takes the view the "low rate limbo" is here to stay, Hershan recalls his days at US fund Fidelity and says there are similarities between the thirst for yield and the exuberance to own the next big thing during the dizzy days of the dot-com bubble. "Up until that point the only way to justify certain valuations was around relative comparisons and we are concerned we are back at that point for some stocks."

HEADLINE: CEO forced into drastic rethink after supermarket sales evaporate
INTRO: Embattled boss Grant O'Brien is sacrificing profits for growth in an environment where short-termism is king.
TEXT:
Embattled boss Grant O'Brien is sacrificing profits for growth in an environment where short-termism is king.

When Grant O'Brien returned to work after a short Christmas break in Tasmania he realised he was going to have to take drastic action to arrest Woolworths' declining sales growth.

The chief executive had been quietly working for four months on plans to pump $500 million into the supermarket business, which had been under-performing rival Coles for years.

But when he sat down and examined the patchy December sales data, O'Brien was alarmed. He undertook a review of the company's core business in January, concluding that the investment planned for the next financial year had to be accelerated.

"This isn't a time to be irrational, it is a time to be disciplined," Mr O'Brien told AFR Weekend, defending the decision after the company's share price fell 9.5 per cent on Friday.

"The market is the market and I knew pretty clearly what the consequences, in the short term at least, would be - that the share price would be affected.

"Was it a tough decision? No, because it was such a clear thing to do."

The decision to sacrifice profit in order to invest back in price and service at Woolworths' 900 supermarkets marked a significant shift in strategy for O'Brien, a former electrician who has worked at the grocer for 25 years and marks four years in the top job this April.

It is a return to the Woolworths strategy of 1999 to 2006, when lower margins helped drive what is known as a "virtuous cycle" of sales growth and cost efficiency - something analysts have been saying the company should have been doing for a while.

O'Brien took his plan to the board for formal approval this week. It was a hard sell - particularly given chairman Ralph Waters had reaffirmed the company's earnings guidance in November - but the board backed his plan.

"It has only been in very recent times that I encouraged the board to look at a different option and bring the investment forward," O'Brien, 53, says.

"We have a very good board and there is not much I do that doesn't get fully tested by the board, I can tell you."

O'Brien's plan became public on Friday when Woolworths cut full-year earnings guidance, announced the departure of its well-regarded supermarkets boss Tjeerd Jegen, and said $500 million of cost savings would be re-invested in lower prices and improving service. Part of O'Brien's defence for the big switch was that the company could have delivered on its 4 per cent to 7 per cent net profit guidance if it wanted to. Instead, he says it is investing for the future.

"We would have wasted six months," he says. "The case for change has been clear and we have been working away quietly behind the scenes to build a war chest we were going to put into the marketplace."

But the rare downgrade was not well received by the market.

Analysts say the company should have been sacrificing profit margins years earlier, rather than waiting until it was lagging Coles' sales by 20 consecutive quarters. They are also concerned about the underperformance of its loss-making Masters hardware operations and Big W.

"I'm really confused right now as to just where supermarkets are at," outspoken Bank of America Merrill Lynch analyst David Errington told O'Brien during a conference call.

"You are stalling in Masters, Big W, and gaming is coming off. When do you say enough is enough?"

Commonwealth Bank of Australia analyst Andrew McLennan says Woolworths has underperformed Coles in sales-per-square-metre growth for several years.

"Woolworths used to have a commanding lead in the market. Arguably, you still have cost leadership given the huge margins, but it seems difficult to understand how a $500 million investment in price can turn this around. You have two major competitors and they will continue to be aggressive."

O'Brien's argument is that the $500 million is just the start. This is expected to increase significantly and he says shoppers will notice a sharp change in prices and service, particularly in fresh food, in the future.

He will also announce a greater emphasis on store refurbishments instead of prioritising new stores, as Woolworths has done more recently, which affects same-store sales.

O'Brien, who will unveil more details at a strategy day in May, wants more time for his new management team to find its feet following the badly timed departure of Jegen, who the company says is stepping down for family reasons. He also denies his own job is on the line, saying the situation needs to be put into perspective.

He says Woolworths is twice as profitable as its competitors and will still increase profits this year.

O'Brien refuses to back down on the hardware strategy, which the market has dubbed a failure, and says the home improvement business is being built for the future.

That is part of O'Brien's problem as he asks the market to take a longer-term view of Woolworths' current problems. Maybe he will do an Alan Joyce and bounce back in a year's time after some tough decisions are implemented. Or maybe he won't.
